opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's already happening, but in a fairly mundane way so far rather than in the dramatic, self-improving-loop sense that people imagine when they talk about the Singularity.

If you look at what AI developers actually do day to day, a lot of it is writing code, debugging, searching the literature, and running and analyzing experiments. Large language models and the coding assistants built on them are now quite helpful for all of that. In my own teams at SingularityNET and on the OpenCog Hyperon project, people use these tools constantly. They write boilerplate, translate between programming languages, suggest fixes, and summarize papers. That's a real productivity boost, maybe tens of percent in some areas and more for certain routine tasks. So in that sense AI is clearly accelerating AI development already.

But I'd distinguish that from AI contributing the core creative insights. LLMs are very good at recombining and interpolating within what humans have already done. They're not yet good at the kind of fundamental conceptual leaps that move the field forward, like coming up with a new cognitive architecture, a new learning paradigm, or a new way of representing knowledge. For that, the humans are still doing the heavy lifting. The AI is more like a really capable research assistant or an army of junior programmers than a co-inventor.

There are also some intermediate cases that are interesting: using machine learning for hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, automated chip design, and using AI to generate synthetic training data. Those are genuine examples of AI improving the substrate that AI runs on, and they compound over time. Hardware gets better partly because of AI-assisted design, which makes training cheaper, which makes better AI.

So how do I assess it? I'd say we're in the early, sub-exponential phase of the feedback loop. The acceleration is real and measurable but incremental. What I'm watching for is the transition point where AI systems can do substantive, original research, where they can formulate hypotheses about how to make themselves smarter, test them, and integrate the results. When that happens, and I think it's plausibly a matter of a few years rather than decades, the dynamics change qualitatively. My own view is that getting there will take more than scaling up current LLMs. You need systems that can actually reason, abstract, and create in a more open-ended way, which is what we're trying to build with neural-symbolic and evolutionary approaches. But once you have something like that, even a fairly modest AGI, the speed at which it can improve AI research could be quite startling.

r001.rationale: It says LLMs and coding assistants help with coding, debugging, literature searches, and experiments, boosting productivity in AI development.

r002.rationale: It describes AI-assisted optimization, chip design, and synthetic data as improvements that compound and advance AI, and says progress will take more than scaling current LLMs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's already happening in a pretty significant way, though not yet in the dramatic, self-amplifying sense that people have in mind when they talk about a hard takeoff or an intelligence explosion. Right now what you've got is AI as a very powerful tool for human AI researchers, rather than AI autonomously doing AI research.

So if you look at what's actually going on in labs, including in our own work at SingularityNET and with OpenCog Hyperon, a huge amount of the day-to-day coding is now being done with LLM assistance. Writing boilerplate, debugging, translating between languages, generating test cases, searching the literature. That's maybe a two-x or three-x speedup on certain kinds of engineering work, and it compounds, because the people building the next generation of systems are using the current generation to go faster. Then you've got things like neural architecture search, AI-driven hyperparameter tuning, AI systems generating synthetic training data for other AI systems, and models being used to evaluate and filter the outputs of other models. All of that is AI accelerating AI, in a fairly concrete sense.

What I don't think we're seeing yet is AI coming up with fundamentally new ideas about how to do AI. The transformer architecture wasn't invented by a transformer. The core conceptual breakthroughs are still coming from humans, and what the machines are doing is accelerating the execution and the exploration around those human-originated ideas. LLMs in particular are very good at recombining what's already in their training data, and not so good at the kind of deep, novel abstraction that leads to a genuinely new paradigm.

Now, I'd say that's the crux of the whole thing. Once you have systems that can do real science, that can form their own hypotheses about cognitive architecture and test them and understand why they worked or didn't, then the feedback loop gets qualitatively different. And I don't think that requires a system that's superhuman at everything. I think an AI that's roughly human-level as a computer scientist, but can run thousands of copies of itself in parallel and never sleeps, already gets you a very steep curve. That's the point where the acceleration stops being a multiplier on human effort and starts being its own thing.

So my overall assessment is: we're in the early, tool-like phase of recursive self-improvement. It's real, it's meaningful, it's compressing timelines, but the loop is still going through human brains at the critical junctures. My guess is that changes within a small number of years rather than decades, and that the transition from where we are now to AGI, and then from AGI to something a lot smarter than us, may be a lot faster than most people are planning for.

r001.rationale: It says LLM assistance speeds day-to-day AI engineering through coding, debugging, test generation, and literature search.

r002.rationale: It describes AI-assisted research and development as a concrete source of faster progress, including architecture search, tuning, and synthetic data generation, separate from any claim about scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s already accelerating it quite a bit, but we should distinguish a few different things. There’s AI helping researchers write code, debug things, search through papers, and analyze experimental results. That makes the whole research process faster, and AI researchers benefit from it just as other programmers and scientists do.

Then there’s AI helping optimize AI systems—searching for architectures, tuning parameters, generating training data. There you already have a feedback loop, in a limited sense. You’re using AI to make better AI.

But that’s different from a system understanding its own design, identifying the fundamental limitations of that design, and inventing a substantially better approach. I don’t think we’ve yet demonstrated that as a robust, open-ended process. The human researchers are still supplying a lot of the conceptual direction and deciding which results actually matter.

The interesting question is when that balance shifts. You don’t necessarily need an AI that can autonomously do every part of research. If it can make a genuinely useful contribution to the hardest conceptual steps, while also doing much of the implementation, the human-AI combination could move dramatically faster. So I think the acceleration is real already, but it’s not yet the full recursive self-improvement process that people tend to imagine.

r001.rationale: It names AI assistance with coding, debugging, paper search, and experimental analysis as ways to speed up the AI research process.

r002.rationale: It describes AI optimizing AI systems and creating a feedback loop, but does not distinguish that driver of progress from scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s already accelerating it in a fairly substantial way, but that’s different from saying we’ve entered a runaway process of recursive self-improvement. A lot of the acceleration is quite practical: AI helps you write code, debug things, search through papers, and explore different approaches more quickly. And AI researchers can use those capabilities just like anyone else.

The harder question is how much AI is contributing to the fundamental conceptual advances. Can it come up with a new learning algorithm, understand why it should work, and design the right experiments to test it? There’s some progress in that direction, but I don’t think we’re at the point where AI is autonomously driving the whole research process.

You also have to distinguish improving an AI system from improving the process that produces AI systems. If you make researchers more productive, that can accelerate development quite a lot without any individual system rewriting its own intelligence. My expectation is that these things will increasingly blend together: humans and AIs doing research jointly, with the AI gradually taking on more of the creative and evaluative work. That could become a very powerful feedback loop, but I wouldn’t infer its speed just from how much better coding assistants have become.

r001.rationale: It names AI assistance with coding, debugging, paper search, and exploring approaches as practical ways researchers can speed up AI development.

r002.rationale: It presents AI-assisted research as an accelerant distinct from a system improving its own intelligence, but does not distinguish that driver from scaling.
